passages.happening:
God speaks to Moses. “Speak to the Israelites and tell them: After you enter the land that I am giving you as a home” (verse 2). Then come instructions for offerings. With every animal brought as a burnt offering or sacrifice, a grain offering of flour mixed with oil and a drink offering of wine are to be added. The larger the animal, the larger the gift that goes with it (verses 4-12).

The same rule holds for the outsider. “The assembly is to have the same statute both for you and for the foreign resident; it is a permanent statute for the generations to come. You and the foreigner shall be the same before the LORD” (verse 15).

A second law follows. When Israel eats the bread of the land, the first of each batch of dough is to be given to the LORD (verses 17-21).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 14 ended in disaster. The people had refused the land. The adults had been sentenced to die in the wilderness. A rash attack had ended in a rout.

Chapter 15 opens, with no bridge at all, on the words ‘After you enter the land that I am giving you as a home’. Placed here, that clause is a promise. The generation that refused will not see the land. Their children will. God is already telling them what to bring from its fields.

The offerings themselves look ahead. Grain, olive oil and wine were the three great crops of Canaan. A people living on manna in the desert had none of them to speak of. The law assumes farms, olive groves and vineyards that Israel does not yet hold. To a people just condemned to wander, every line says that the wandering will end.

The phrase ‘for the generations to come’ returns again and again in the chapter. It assumes a future.

So does the place given to the foreigner. The Hebrew word is ger, a person from elsewhere living among Israel. Four times in this chapter the native and the foreigner are set side by side under one law. In worship they ‘shall be the same before the LORD’. Israel has just failed badly, and the law that follows the failure widens the door.

The gift from the first of the dough brought the same thought into every kitchen. Before a family ate bread from the land, a portion was lifted up to God. Each batch was a reminder of who had given the land.
passages.later:
Paul uses the picture of the first portion of dough when he writes of Israel and the nations: “If the first part of the dough is holy, so is the whole batch” (Romans 11:16).

And he tells believers from the nations what this chapter's one law for native and foreigner pointed toward: “Therefore you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household” (Ephesians 2:19).
passages.asks: The first words God spoke after the sentence of forty years were about life in the land. Ask whether, after a failure of your own, you can hear God still speaking to you about a future. And ask who the outsider is in your place of worship, and whether they stand the same before the LORD in the way they are treated.

passages.happening:
The law turns to sin. If the whole congregation goes astray ‘unintentionally’, an offering is to be brought. “The priest is to make atonement for the whole congregation of Israel, so that they may be forgiven” (verse 25). If one person sins unintentionally, that person brings a goat, ‘and when atonement has been made for him, he will be forgiven’ (verse 28). The law is the same for native and foreigner (verse 29).

Then comes the other case. “But the person who sins defiantly, whether a native or foreigner, blasphemes the LORD. That person shall be cut off from among his people” (verse 30). “He shall certainly be cut off, because he has despised the word of the LORD and broken His commandment; his guilt remains on him” (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
A reader needs one distinction to follow this passage. The Hebrew word for the first kind of sin, shegagah, means an error: a wrong done by mistake or without knowing. It comes seven times in this chapter. The offerings were built for such sins. An animal was brought, the priest made atonement, and the promise was plain: ‘he will be forgiven’. That promise is given three times in eight verses. The word for forgiving is the one Moses used when he begged God to pardon the people in chapter 14.

The other kind is described with a picture. The Hebrew speaks, word for word, of sinning with a raised hand. It is the picture of a fist lifted against God. It does not mean a sin done on purpose in a weak moment. It means open, settled contempt: a person who knows what God has said and has ‘despised the word of the LORD’.

For that, no offering is named. The offerings were a way back for people who wanted one. They were not a device for someone who had thrown off God altogether and meant to stay that way.

What ‘cut off’ means is debated. Some take it as a death penalty carried out by the community. Others take it as an early death, or the end of a family line, at God's own hand. Later Jewish tradition generally understood it as something God himself carries out.

It matters where this law stands. Israel has just sinned with a raised hand at Kadesh. And yet in chapter 14 Moses prayed, and God pardoned. Even the gravest revolt in the book was met with a mediator's prayer and forgiveness. The law states what defiance deserves. The story beside it shows that God's mercy reached further than the offerings did.
passages.later:
Hebrews describes the high priest as one who “is able to deal gently with those who are ignorant and misguided, since he himself is beset by weakness” (Hebrews 5:2). That is the provision of verses 22 to 29.

Hebrews also echoes verses 30 and 31 when it warns those who ‘deliberately go on sinning’ after knowing the truth (Hebrews 10:26). The warning is written to the church.

Peter told the crowd in Jerusalem, “And now, brothers, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did your leaders” (Acts 3:17), and called them to turn back so that their sins might be wiped away.
passages.hard:
Does this passage mean that a sin done knowingly cannot be forgiven?

No. That is not what ‘defiantly’ means here, and the rest of the Bible shows as much. David took another man's wife and arranged the man's death, knowing full well what he did. No sacrifice was named for that. He prayed, “For You do not delight in sacrifice, or I would bring it” (Psalm 51:16), and he was forgiven (2 Samuel 12:13). Peter denied Jesus three times with his eyes open and was restored.

The sin of verse 30 is the lifted fist: a settled, open rejection of God by someone who does not want to come back. A person who is grieved by a sin, and afraid of what it means, is doing the opposite of raising a fist. The note on Hebrews 10 takes up the same question.

If you are a person whose conscience never rests, who keeps checking whether you have really believed, hear John's words: “Even if our hearts condemn us, God is greater than our hearts, and He knows all things” (1 John 3:20). Such fear can be part of anxiety or a habit of the mind, and that is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust, and if the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The law promised three times that a person who went astray and came back would be forgiven. Ask what wrong you have done without meaning to that you have never brought to God or put right. And ask whether there is anywhere in your life where the hand is raised: where you know what God has said and have decided not to care.

passages.t: The man who gathered wood on the Sabbath
passages.happening:
“While the Israelites were in the wilderness, a man was found gathering wood on the Sabbath day” (verse 32). Those who found him bring him to Moses, Aaron and the congregation. And ‘because it had not been declared what should be done to him, they placed him in custody’ (verse 34).

“And the LORD said to Moses, ‘The man must surely be put to death. The whole congregation is to stone him outside the camp’” (verse 35). The congregation does so (verse 36).
passages.hearers:
This is one of the hardest short stories in the book, and it should be read honestly. A man is put to death for picking up sticks. The story gives him no words and tells us nothing of his reasons.

Three things in the text help a reader see what the story is doing, though they do not make it easy.

The first is where it stands. It comes straight after the law about sin with a raised hand. Most readers take it as an example of that law. The Sabbath was not an obscure rule. Israel had been taught it with the manna, when no bread fell on the seventh day (Exodus 16). Its penalty had been stated (Exodus 31:14-15). Lighting a fire on the Sabbath had been named in particular (Exodus 35:3), and a man gathering wood was presumably getting ready to light one. On this reading the act was public and knowing.

The second is what the Sabbath meant. It was the sign of the covenant between God and Israel (Exodus 31:13). In a camp where God himself lived in the middle as king, to break it openly was more like treason than like a private lapse.

The third is the restraint. Nobody acted in anger. The man was held, and Moses waited for God to rule. This is one of several stories in the five books where a case the law had not fully settled is brought to God.

Many readers find all this true and still not enough. The story stays hard, and these notes do not pretend otherwise.
passages.later:
Jesus kept the Sabbath, and he opposed rules that made it a burden. “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. Therefore, the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27-28).

Paul writes to a church that included people who were not Jews, “Therefore let no one judge you by what you eat or drink, or with regard to a feast, a New Moon, or a Sabbath. These are a shadow of the things to come, but the body that casts it belongs to Christ” (Colossians 2:16-17).
passages.hard:
Does this story mean that people who break the Sabbath, or God's other commands, should be punished today?

No. Christians have generally held that the penalties of Israel's law belonged to Israel's own situation, as a nation living under God's direct rule with his tent in its midst. They are not carried into the church, and they are no pattern for any court or government now. The furthest the New Testament takes the church's own discipline is to put a person out of the fellowship, with the hope of winning them back (1 Corinthians 5).

Christians differ on how the Sabbath command applies now. Some keep Sunday as the Christian Sabbath, some keep the seventh day, and some hold that the day was a shadow fulfilled in Christ and leave it to conscience. None of them reads this story as a model for punishing anyone.

No one may use this passage to threaten, shame or harm a person for what they do on any day of the week. What the story still presses on a reader is that God is not indifferent to being openly defied.
passages.asks: The story is hard, and the community that carried it out first stopped and waited to hear from God. Ask how quickly you pass judgment on another person's conduct, and whether you wait to hear before you speak. And ask what the gift of a day of rest has become in your own life: a burden, a thing ignored, or a gift.

passages.happening:
God gives Israel something to wear. They are to make ‘tassels for the corners of their garments, with a blue cord on each tassel’ (verse 38).

The reason follows. “These will serve as tassels for you to look at, so that you may remember all the commandments of the LORD, that you may obey them and not prostitute yourselves by following your own heart and your own eyes” (verse 39).

“I am the LORD your God who brought you out of the land of Egypt to be your God. I am the LORD your God” (verse 41).
passages.hearers:
After the law about defiance and the story of the Sabbath-breaker, the chapter ends with a help for the wandering heart.

In the ancient world the hem of a garment said who a person was. Decorated hems appear on the clothes of important people in ancient art, and a hem could stand for its owner. David once cut off the corner of King Saul's robe (1 Samuel 24). Israel is told to put a sign on the edge of its ordinary clothes.

The cord was blue. That was the color of the tabernacle's curtains and of the high priest's robe. The dye was costly and was made from sea snails. So every Israelite, man or woman of no special rank, carried on their clothing a thread of the sanctuary's color. The whole people was marked as belonging to God.

The purpose is memory. A person would see the tassel many times a day and remember the commandments. And verse 39 says what the tassels guard against: ‘following your own heart and your own eyes’. The Hebrew verb for ‘following’ here is the one used for the scouts who went to explore the land. The scouts had looked with their own eyes and come back with unbelief. The tassels are given so that Israel's eyes will fall on something else.

The law closes with God's name said twice, and with a reminder of the exodus. The commands come from the God who rescued them. They are told to remember because they belong to him already.

Jewish men still wear these tassels, called tzitzit. They are often all white, because the way of making the old blue dye was lost for centuries. And verses 37 to 41 became the third paragraph of the Shema, the confession recited morning and evening in Jewish prayer.
passages.later:
Jesus wore them. A woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years ‘came up behind Him and touched the fringe of His cloak’ (Matthew 9:20), and she was healed.

He also warned teachers who made their tassels long in order to be seen: “All their deeds are done for men to see. They broaden their phylacteries and lengthen their tassels” (Matthew 23:5). A sign given to help people remember God can be turned into a way of being noticed.
passages.asks: God gave Israel something to look at many times a day, so that their eyes would not lead them. Ask what your eyes rest on most often in a day, and where it leads your heart. And ask what simple, daily reminder would help you remember whose you are.
